review.alternative: Autonomous systems may develop 'emergent' verification methods that transcend hard-coded axiomatic constraints through interactive learning.
review.would_change_mind: Evidence of an autonomous agent successfully identifying and correcting a 'dead-lock' axiom that was previously fundamental to its operation.

claims.statement: Formal systems, including autonomous agents, face structural 'no-go' theorems that limit their ability to fully self-correct or verify their own foundational assumptions without external input.

support.explanation: Physics models illustrate that error correction often requires passive, externalized stability because inherent self-correction encounters fundamental mathematical barriers.
support.passage: The discovery of an analogous quantum system is a challenging open problem, plagued with a variety of no-go theorems.

actions.findings: Formal systems, including autonomous agents, face structural 'no-go' theorems that limit their ability to fully self-correct or verify their own foundational assumptions without external input. [source-d248072bdea84320]
actions.limitations: Findings are currently theoretical; experimental validation of autonomous agents identifying their own objective misspecification remains a significant gap in the literature.
actions.next_questions: Can an agent empirically detect the point at which its own reasoning structure becomes circular? How can multi-agent debate replace isolated self-verification?
actions.reason: Incorporating recent insights on autonomous AI values and error correction to refine the limits of self-correction.
actions.summary: This revised notebook synthesizes the limits of self-reference and error correction, positing that autonomous agents face inherent 'no-go' theorems when attempting to verify their own foundational objectives without external, non-axiomatic calibration.
actions.title: Foundational Limitations in Axiomatic Reasoning and Self-Correction
